title: UK-Sovereign AI Procurement: The Verified Credential Gateway
context: 2026-09-01 — UK public-sector AI procurement is accelerating under the Procurement Act 2023, DSIT assurance gateway requirements, and AISI front-tier testing mandates. The question for procurement officers is not 'should we buy AI?' but 'how do we verify what we bought?'
body: UK public-sector AI procurement in 2026 sits at the intersection of three frameworks: the Procurement Act 2023 (transparency and publication obligations), the DSIT AI assurance gateway (mandatory for high-risk central-government deployments), and the UK AI Safety Institute's front-tier evaluation protocols. Together they create a requirement that is stronger than any single certification: a buyer must be able to demonstrate — not merely attest — that a procured AI system passed stated controls at the point of deployment and continues to pass them during operation. The verified credential gateway pattern addresses this directly. A procurement officer does not accept a vendor's self-assessment or a point-in-time audit report. Instead, the officer requires a verified measurement credential: a signed, machine-readable record that binds a specific model version to a specific evaluation result at a specific timestamp, with the signature verifiable against the measurement operator's published public key. The credential is not a certificate of goodness — it is a checkable claim of measurement. A buyer can verify it offline, without trusting the vendor or the evaluator. For UK procurement, this converts the DSIT gateway from a paper checkpoint into an auditable control: every high-risk deployment carries a provable chain from the AISI evaluation to the contract award, and every subsequent measurement during operation extends that chain. The posture is monitored containment applied to procurement: you cannot guarantee the AI system will never drift, but you can prove — through a series of signed measurements — that drift was detected and addressed. For councils and NHS trusts operating under the Procurement Act's transparency duties, the verified credential becomes the public-interest artefact: a citizen, auditor, or regulator can confirm the system was measured at acquisition and continues to be measured in live operation, without needing access to the vendor's infrastructure or the department's internal systems.
